essays.stem: Explain how you would use styles, a table of contents, headers, footers and page numbers to produce a professional long document, such as a staff handbook.
essays.modelAnswer: First I type the text and apply heading styles to every heading: Heading 1 for chapter titles, such as 'Safety rules', and Heading 2 for the parts inside each chapter. The normal text uses the Normal style. Using styles makes every heading look the same, and if I change a style once, every heading of that kind changes. Next I put the cursor at the start of the document and insert an automatic table of contents. The program builds it from the heading styles, with the right page numbers. I add a header with the business name and a footer with page numbers that are inserted as a field, so they update by themselves. I can add the date or the document's title to the footer too. If I add or move text later, I use the Update Table command so the contents page stays correct. Finally I check it in Print Preview and save it, also as a PDF for sharing.
markingPoints: Applies heading styles to headings and explains the benefit (same look, changed in one place)
Inserts an automatic table of contents built from the heading styles
Adds a header with suitable text such as the business name
Adds automatic page numbers in the footer
Updates the table of contents after changes and checks the layout before saving or sharing

essays.stem: Describe the steps of a mail merge to send a personal letter to each client on a list.
essays.modelAnswer: First I prepare the data source: a table or spreadsheet with one row for each client and a column for each detail, such as title, first name, last name, address and the date of their last visit. I check the list for spelling mistakes and empty cells. Next I open a new letter in the word processor and start the mail merge, choosing letters. I connect the letter to the data source. I type the parts of the letter that are the same for everyone, and insert merge fields where the personal details go, such as the client's first name in the greeting and their address at the top. I use Preview to look at several letters and check that the details appear correctly and the spacing is right. Then I finish the merge, either printing the letters or making a new document of all the letters to check first. Finally I save the main letter and the data source so they can be used again.
markingPoints: Prepares and checks a data source with one row per client and a column per detail
Starts the mail merge and connects the letter to the data source
Types the common text and inserts merge fields in the right places
Previews several letters to check details and layout
Completes the merge (print or new document) and saves the letter and data source

essays.stem: Explain how you would build a simple quotation in a spreadsheet, using formulas to work out the line totals, the subtotal, GCT and the total.
essays.modelAnswer: I set up columns for the item, the quantity, the unit price in J$ and the line total. In the first line-total cell I type a formula that multiplies the quantity by the unit price, for example =B2*C2, and then use the fill handle to copy it down for every item. Below the list, I use =SUM to add up all the line totals to give the subtotal. I type the GCT rate, at the current rate given by my supervisor, into its own labelled cell, such as F1, so it can be changed easily if the rate changes. The GCT amount is the subtotal multiplied by the rate cell, using an absolute reference such as $F$1 so it does not move if the formula is copied. The total is the subtotal plus the GCT. I format the money cells as currency with two decimal places, check one line with a calculator, and add the business name, the customer's name and the date before saving and printing.
markingPoints: Sets up clear columns for item, quantity, unit price and line total
Uses a multiply formula for each line total and copies it with the fill handle
Uses SUM for the subtotal
Puts the GCT rate (current rate) in its own cell and uses an absolute reference
Works out the total, formats money as currency and checks the result

essays.stem: Explain the difference between relative and absolute cell references, and give an example of when each is used.
essays.modelAnswer: A relative reference, such as B2, changes when a formula is copied to another cell. If cell D2 holds =B2*C2 and I copy it down to D3, it becomes =B3*C3. This is what I want when each row works out its own total, for example the line totals in a price list of cables or salon products. An absolute reference has dollar signs, such as $F$1, and does not change when the formula is copied. It always points to the same cell. This is used when every row must use one fixed value, such as a discount rate or the GCT rate kept in one cell. For example, in E2 the formula =D2*$F$1 works out the GCT for one line. When I copy it down, D2 changes to D3, D4 and so on, but $F$1 stays the same. If I forgot the dollar signs, the formula would point to empty cells and give wrong answers. A mixed reference, such as $F1, fixes only the column or the row.
markingPoints: Explains that a relative reference changes when copied
Gives a suitable relative example, such as line totals
Explains that an absolute reference ($F$1) stays fixed when copied
Gives a suitable absolute example, such as a fixed rate cell
Explains what goes wrong without the $ signs (or mentions mixed references)

essays.stem: Describe how to make a chart from spreadsheet data, and explain how to choose the right type of chart.
essays.modelAnswer: First I set out the data in a clear table with headings, for example the months in one column and the sales in J$ in the next. I select the headings and the data, then use the Insert menu to choose a chart. Choosing the right type matters. A column or bar chart is best for comparing amounts, such as the sales of different products. A line chart is best for showing how something changes over time, such as monthly sales over a year. A pie chart is best for showing how parts make up a whole, such as each service's share of a salon's total sales, and it should have only a few slices. After inserting the chart, I add a clear title and axis titles with units, and a legend if there is more than one series. I check that the chart shows the data correctly, move it so it does not cover the table, and save the file.
markingPoints: Sets out the data in a table with headings and selects it
Inserts the chart from the menu
Column or bar for comparing amounts; line for change over time
Pie for parts of a whole, with only a few slices
Adds a title, axis titles or legend and checks the chart is correct

essays.stem: Explain how sorting, filtering and conditional formatting can help a business manage a stock list.
essays.modelAnswer: A stock list might have columns for the item, the supplier, the number in stock, the reorder level and the price. Sorting puts the rows in order by one column. For example, sorting by the number in stock, smallest first, puts the items that are running low at the top, and sorting by supplier groups the items from each supplier together, which helps when ordering. The whole table must be selected so that each row stays together. Filtering shows only the rows that match a choice and hides the rest without deleting them. For example, I can filter to show only items from one supplier, or only hair products, then clear the filter to see everything again. Conditional formatting changes the look of a cell when its value meets a rule. For example, the stock cell can turn red when the number in stock falls to the reorder level or below, so low items stand out at a glance. Together these tools save time and help stop the business running out of stock.
markingPoints: Sorting puts rows in order, with a suitable example
Selects the whole table so rows stay together
Filtering shows only matching rows without deleting the rest, with an example
Conditional formatting changes a cell's look when a rule is met, such as low stock turning red
Explains the benefit: saves time and prevents running out of stock

essays.stem: Describe how you would make a clear presentation to train new staff, using the slide master, layouts, transitions and speaker notes.
essays.modelAnswer: First I plan the main points and put them in order, one idea to each slide. I use the slide master to set the design for every slide in one place: the background, the fonts, the colours, and the business name and slide number in the footer. This keeps all the slides looking the same. For each slide I choose a suitable layout, such as Title and Content or Two Content, so text and pictures sit neatly. I keep to a few short points on each slide, in a large clear font with good contrast, and add clear photos or diagrams, such as a picture of a safety sign or a correct product display. I use one simple transition between slides and only a few animations, so they do not distract. I write what I want to say in the speaker notes, where the audience will not see it. Finally I run the slide show from the beginning to check the order, the spelling and the timing.
markingPoints: Plans the content with one main idea per slide
Uses the slide master to set a consistent design and footer
Chooses suitable layouts and keeps text short, large and clear, with pictures
Uses simple transitions and few animations
Uses speaker notes and checks the show in Slide Show view

essays.stem: Explain the main parts of a database, using a client database for a salon or an electrical contractor as an example.
essays.modelAnswer: A database stores information in tables. A client table holds the details of all the clients. Each column is a field, which holds one kind of detail, such as first name, last name, phone number, address or date of last visit. Each row is a record, which holds all the details for one client. Each record has a primary key, such as a client number, which is different for every client, so two clients with the same name can still be told apart. A form gives a clear screen layout for entering or viewing one record at a time, which makes typing in a new client easier and reduces mistakes. A query searches the table for records that match a rule, for example all clients in Mandeville, or all customers whose last job was more than a year ago. A report sets out the results neatly for printing, for example a list of clients to call with a reminder.
markingPoints: Table: stores the data, such as all the clients
Field: one kind of detail; record: all details for one client
Primary key: a unique value, such as a client number
Form: for entering or viewing one record at a time
Query to search for matching records and report to print results, with examples

essays.stem: Explain how you would protect and back up work files, especially files that hold client details.
essays.modelAnswer: Files with client details, such as names, phone numbers and treatment notes, are private and must be protected. I keep them in the right work folder, not on the desktop, and I give them clear names. I protect important files with a strong password and lock my computer when I leave it. I share files only with the staff who need them, and I do not send them to my personal email or phone. I do not leave printed copies lying around, and I shred them when they are no longer needed. To avoid losing work, I save often while I work and keep a backup copy in a second place, such as the business's cloud storage or an external drive kept in a safe place, as the business's rules say. I check that the backup works by opening a file from it now and then. I also keep the computer's security software up to date and do not open unknown attachments.
markingPoints: Explains that client details are private and must be protected
Uses passwords, locks the screen and limits sharing to staff who need the files
Stores files in the right folder with clear names and handles printed copies safely
Saves often and keeps a backup in a second safe place, checking it works
Keeps security software up to date and avoids unknown attachments

essays.stem: Explain how a team can review a document using comments and Track Changes, and how a chart from a spreadsheet can be kept up to date inside a report.
essays.modelAnswer: When a team reviews a document, the writer turns on Track Changes before sharing it. Every change that a reviewer makes, such as a deleted word or new sentence, is then shown in colour with the reviewer's name. Reviewers use comments to ask questions or make suggestions in the margin without changing the text, for example 'Check this price'. The writer reads each change and chooses Accept or Reject, and answers or deletes each comment. When all changes are dealt with, Track Changes is turned off and the final copy is saved with a new version name. To put a spreadsheet chart into a report, I copy the chart and use Paste Special to paste it as a linked object, not as a picture. Then, when the figures in the spreadsheet change, the chart in the report can be updated. I must keep both files in the same place, and check the link before printing.
markingPoints: Turns on Track Changes so each edit shows with the reviewer's name
Comments are used for questions or suggestions without changing the text
The writer accepts or rejects each change and deals with comments, then saves a final version
Pastes the chart as a linked object (Paste Special), not as a picture
Explains that the linked chart updates when the figures change and the files must stay together

practical1.title: Build a priced quotation in a spreadsheet, with formulas, conditional formatting and a chart
practical1.brief: As a group, use a spreadsheet program on the Centre's computer to build a quotation from one of the assessor's scenario cards: (a) materials to wire a small bedroom (outlets, switches, boxes, conduit, cable, breaker), or (b) a salon's monthly order of products (shampoo, conditioner, treatments, gloves, towels). The card gives the items, the quantities and the unit prices in J$. Share the work so that each member does at least one stage at the computer while the others watch and check: (1) make a group folder, start a new file and set up the headings: item, quantity, unit price (J$) and line total, (2) type in the items, quantities and prices, (3) write the line-total formula and copy it down with the fill handle, then use SUM for the subtotal, (4) put the GCT rate the instructor gives (the current rate) in its own labelled cell and work out the GCT with an absolute reference, then the grand total, (5) format money as currency, add conditional formatting to highlight any line over J$10 000, sort the list by line total, and make a column chart of the line totals with a title. In a group of 4, one member does two stages. Each member then explains one formula to the assessor. Save with a clear file name and print or save as a PDF. Take a screenshot or photo at each stage below and add them to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A computer with a spreadsheet program, connected to a printer
A scenario card with the items, quantities and unit prices in J$
The GCT rate from the instructor (the current rate)
The Centre's shared folder or a USB flash drive
A phone or camera for photos and screenshots
photos: The group folder and the new file with the column headings
The items, quantities and prices typed in
The line-total formula shown in the formula bar, and the column filled down
The GCT rate cell and the GCT formula with the absolute reference in the formula bar
The conditional formatting showing, and the list sorted by line total
The finished column chart with its title
The printed or PDF quotation next to the screen
checklist: Set up clear headings and typed data accurately
Wrote a correct line-total formula and copied it with the fill handle
Used SUM correctly for the subtotal
Used a separate rate cell and an absolute reference for GCT
Formatted money as currency and applied conditional formatting correctly
Sorted the whole table without breaking the rows apart
Made a suitable chart with a clear title
Explained one formula clearly to the assessor
Saved the file with a clear name in the right folder
safety: Keep drinks and food away from the computer
Keep cables off the floor where people walk
Sit with good posture and take a short break if working for a long time
Do not open unknown files or attachments; follow the Centre's computer rules

practical2.title: Produce mail-merged letters and a short styled booklet in a word processor
practical2.brief: As a group, use the Centre's word processor to make two pieces of work for a small business: a home electrical service, or a hair and beauty salon (choose one). Part A, mail merge: make a data source of 6 made-up clients (title, first name, last name, address, service, date) in a table or spreadsheet; write a short reminder letter; insert merge fields for the client's name, address and service; preview the letters and complete the merge. Part B, booklet: make a 3-page customer information booklet (for example 'Using electricity safely at home' or 'Caring for your hair after a treatment'), with heading styles for every heading, an automatic table of contents, a header with the business name, page numbers in the footer, one table and one picture. Then one member turns on Track Changes and another adds two comments and one change, and the group accepts or rejects them. Share the work so that each member does at least one stage at the computer while the others check it, and each member explains their stage to the assessor. Save both with clear names and save the booklet as a PDF. Use made-up names only, never real client details. Take a screenshot or photo at each stage below and add them to the group's practical. Hand in the merged letters and the PDF once for the whole group.
materials: A computer with a word processor (and spreadsheet program if used for the data source), connected to a printer
The task card from the assessor with the made-up client details
Pictures from the Centre's own photo folder
The Centre's shared folder or a USB flash drive
A phone or camera for photos and screenshots

The preview showing one merged letter with a client's details
The booklet with heading styles and the automatic table of contents
The header and the page numbers in the footer
Track Changes and comments showing in the margin
The finished PDF booklet and the merged letters
checklist: Made a correct data source with one row per client and clear column headings
Inserted merge fields in the right places and previewed the letters
Completed the merge so each letter shows the right details
Applied heading styles and inserted an automatic table of contents
Added a header and automatic page numbers in the footer
Used Track Changes and comments, and accepted or rejected the changes
Saved both files with clear names and saved the booklet as a PDF

Keep drinks and food away from the computer
